title: The Words on Yue Fei's Back
text:
Yue Fei was a general of the Southern Song dynasty who fought the Jurchen Jin invaders who had overrun northern China in the 1120s. He rose from a poor farming family to command one of the most effective armies of the age, and won a series of victories that brought him close to recovering lost territory.

At court, however, the chief minister Qin Hui favored peace with the Jin. In 1140 Yue Fei was recalled from the front by a series of urgent orders. He was arrested, charged with treason on flimsy grounds, and put to death in prison in 1142, at thirty-nine.

The official History of Song records that when he was interrogated, Yue Fei tore open his robe to show his interrogators four characters deeply tattooed across his back: "Serve the country with utmost loyalty."

Later tradition, most fully in popular novels and plays written centuries afterward, explains the tattoo with a story about his mother. As her son prepared to go to war, she is said to have pricked the words into his skin with a needle and ink so that he would never forget his duty. The scene of the mother tattooing her son became one of the best known images in Chinese culture. Yue Fei was rehabilitated twenty years after his death and is honored at a temple beside West Lake in Hangzhou.
lesson: Parents give children values to carry long after they leave home. What we teach them to hold dear can guide them in their hardest hour.
source: History of Song (Song Shi), biography of Yue Fei; later popular tradition
caveat: The tattoo is recorded in the official history, but the story that his mother made it comes from later tradition.
